title: The Invisible Conversation Behind Every Tap
description: Every important action in an online product is a conversation between systems. Follow one request from tap to response, learn why servers never trust the screen, and see how products handle waiting, failure and trying again.

objectives.label: Describe a user action as a structured message: what leaves the device, where it is sent, and what comes back
Explain why a server validates every request, and tell authentication apart from authorization
Design for waiting, duplicates, conflicts and lost connections instead of trusting the screen
Match a feature to a communication pattern: one request, a command, an upload, a background job or live updates

blocks.text:
Two students each see "1 ticket remaining" and press Buy at almost the same time. Both screens believe the ticket is available. Neither screen can decide, because each device knows only part of what is happening.

Student A's browser does not know what Student B is doing. Student B's browser does not know whether the ticket is already reserved. A system both students talk to must decide.

When multiple users share or compete for the same information, the browser cannot be the final authority. The shared server owns the truth.

blocks.alt: The path of one action from the interface through a network to a remote system and back to the interface
blocks.caption: The screen is only the visible edge of this conversation.
steps: The user does something
The interface turns the action into a message
The message travels through a network
A remote system receives it and checks whether it is valid
It reads data, changes data, or performs computation
It creates a response
The response travels back
The interface decides what to show

blocks.text:
Each browser sends a request and waits. It does not get to mark the ticket sold. The server asks the questions neither phone can answer: is the ticket still available, is this person signed in, has this exact request already been processed, and what should this student be told? Then it writes the result once.

Student A's request can win. The server marks the ticket unavailable and returns success. Student B, a moment later, gets a conflict: the ticket is gone. Both screens were honest about what they had seen. Only the server had seen both buyers.

The screen is the visible edge of that conversation. The product designer defines what leaves the device, what the server verifies, and what each student gets back.

blocks.question: Both browsers show the last ticket as available and both buyers press Buy. Who decides which one gets it?

options.label: Each browser keeps its own version of who won
A shared server receives both requests, reserves the ticket once, and rejects the second
The ticket is sold to both students

blocks.explanation: When multiple users share or compete for the same information, the browser cannot be the final authority. The shared server owns the truth: it reserves the ticket for one request and sends a different answer back to the other.

blocks.title: Punchline
blocks.text: Every important action in an online product is a conversation between systems, and the product designer must define that conversation.

lessons.title: What the message says, and what gets believed

slides.title: A button does not send the screen

blocks.text:
Pressing Buy does not send the screen anywhere. The application builds a small structured message, called the payload, with named fields such as ticketId, eventId, quantity and requestId.

Without names the server would receive 9082, 441, 1, 7719 and have to guess what each number means. Named fields let both systems agree on what each value is.

When you tell an agent to "send the form," you still must name which fields leave the device, which are required, and which exist only for display.

blocks.alt: A URL broken into its communication rules, its domain name, and a path naming a specific capability
blocks.caption: https://api.stagepass.app/events/441/tickets/9082/reserve
steps: https:// - the communication rules; HTTPS protects the message while it travels
api.stagepass.app - a human-readable domain; DNS finds the network address behind it
/events/441/tickets/9082/reserve - the path, naming the exact capability the app wants to use

blocks.text:
The message needs an address, not only a body. https://api.stagepass.app/events/441/tickets/9082/reserve is one. https names the rules for the trip, including that the contents should not travel as openly readable traffic. api.stagepass.app is a domain, a human name for a destination. The browser looks up which network address that name points at, then sends the message there.

The path gets more specific as it continues: the events collection, event 441, its tickets, ticket 9082, and the reserve action. An endpoint is that address for one capability. Reserve, cancel, upload, and login are different capabilities. A path called /saveData hides which data, for which user, and under which rules.

A readable path is the conversation. POST /tournaments/88/matches/14/report-result reports one match. GET /users/42/notifications reads. If you cannot name the capability from the path, the architecture is still vague.

blocks.question: A request arrives containing only '9082, 441, 1, 7719' with no field names. What is the problem?

options.label: Nothing; numbers travel faster than names
The server cannot tell which value is the ticket, the event, the quantity or the attempt; named fields let both systems agree
The message is too long to send
Servers ignore messages made of numbers

blocks.explanation: Structure is what makes a message meaningful. Named fields such as ticketId and quantity let the sending and receiving systems agree on what each value means; bare numbers are just guesses.

blocks.title: A request is not automatically trusted
steps: Does this ticket exist? The server looks up the ticket, not the screen claim.
Is it still available? Shared truth lives on the server, not in either browser.
Is the event still active, and is the user signed in?
Is this user allowed to buy it? Authorization is separate from knowing who they are.
Has this exact request already been processed? A requestId prevents double sales on retry.
Does the server's stored price match the transaction? Never trust a price the client invents.
Only after those checks does the server reserve once and return success or conflict.

blocks.title: Punchline
blocks.text: Authentication checks the name tag. Authorization checks the permission.

Authentication answers who this is. Authorization answers what this person may do. A student can be signed in as Maya and still be forbidden to delete the school's event. The server checks both on every important request, including one that never came from a button on the screen.

Hiding Delete is interface behavior. Someone can send that request by hand. If the server trusts the screen, the hidden button is not a lock.

The browser can also name a price. A ticket does not cost one dollar because the payload says so. The server reads the price it stored. A request is a claim. The checks turn the claim into a decision.

A user presses Save and the interface immediately shows Saved. The request failed. The word on the screen changed, and the server has no new row. The screen and the server are not the same system, so a confident screen can lie.

An optimistic update shows the result you hope for before the answer arrives, which makes the product feel fast. If the server rejects the request, or never answers, the screen has to take that promise back and show what actually happened.

Each ending is a different fact. Loading means the request left and nothing has come back. Success means the server confirmed it. Empty means the request worked and there was nothing to show. A validation error means the message itself was unacceptable. Unauthorized means the person is not signed in. Forbidden means the server knows who they are and still refuses. A conflict means the action clashes with the current truth, such as a ticket someone else just took. A timeout or an offline device means no usable answer arrived. The happy path is only one of those screens.

blocks.alt: The states a request can end in, from loading and success through empty, errors, conflict, timeout and offline
blocks.caption: Every important request needs a designed answer for each of these.
steps: Loading - sent, no answer yet
Success - the server confirmed it
Empty - it worked, but there is nothing to show
Validation error - the request was missing or unacceptable
Unauthorized - the user is not signed in
Forbidden - the user is known but not allowed
Not found - the item does not exist
Conflict - the request clashes with the current state
Timeout or offline - no usable answer arrived

blocks.text:
The student presses Buy and nothing seems to happen, so they press Buy again. The first request was only slow. The server now has two purchase messages for the same ticket. Charging twice would punish the wait.

The payload can carry a request id such as purchase-attempt-7719. When that id arrives again, the server recognizes the attempt, skips a second sale, and returns the result it already produced. Retrying the same action should not perform it twice. The same rule covers reservations, submitted assignments, invitations, and refunds.

Disabling the button while the request runs helps a person who is still looking at the page. It does not stop a refresh, a second device, or a message the network sends again. The server has to recognize the duplicate too.

blocks.question: A student presses Buy, nothing seems to happen, and presses Buy again. How does the server avoid selling the same ticket twice?

options.label: The second click is physically impossible
Each request carries a unique request ID, so the server recognizes the retried request and returns the existing result
The server refuses all repeated requests
The student is charged twice and refunded later

blocks.explanation: Retrying the same action should not perform it twice. A unique request ID lets the server recognize that purchase-attempt-7719 was already processed and return the same result. Disabling the button helps, but the server must guard too, because buttons cannot stop resent requests.

slides.title: Not every feature has the same conversation

blocks.text:
Opening an album is one request and one answer: title, artist, and the first 20 tracks, not every comment and every listener. When the person scrolls, the app asks for the next 20. That is pagination. Sending the whole library on the first open makes the product slower and more expensive for information nobody has asked to see yet.

Equipping a helmet is a different conversation. The device says equip item 712. The server checks that this player owns it, that it is a helmet, and what was equipped before, then stores the loadout and replies with the confirmed one. If the phone were the authority, a player could equip a paid item by editing the page. A video upload is different again: a large file, visible progress, and a processing status, because the bytes and the finished clip are not the same moment.

Generating an image starts work that finishes later. The app either asks again until the job is done, which is polling, or receives the result as it is produced, which is streaming. A typing indicator is a live event on an open connection. It is not a row you keep. Match the feature to the conversation before you ask an agent to build one shape for all of them.

blocks.title: Punchline
blocks.text: A web product is not several screens connected by buttons. It is several systems connected by carefully designed conversations.
